newsitem.title: VATICAN: Pope treads delicate path on Lebanon visit.
newsitem.headline: Pope treads delicate path on Lebanon visit.

text.p: Pope John Paul will tread a delicate path through Lebanon's complex denominational politics when he visits Beirut at the weekend, three years after cancelling a trip for security reasons.
Lebanon was devastated from 1975 to 1990 by civil war -- a conflict fed by rivalries among religious communities as the long dominant Christians came in modern times to be outnumbered by Moslems.
The Pope's May 10 and 11 pilgrimage to Lebanon will be the first to the Middle East for the 76-year-old Roman Catholic leader.

It comes four weeks after a groundbreaking visit to Bosnia, where, in a major security scare just hours before his arrival in Sarajevo, anti-tank mines were found planted on the route of the Pope's motorcade.

Vatican sources said all police and army leave in Lebanon had been cancelled for the Polish-born Pope's visit, at which he will preside over the ceremonial close of a synod on the future of the Lebanese Church held at the Vatican in 1995.

It will take the Pontiff to Beirut, the presidential palace at Baabda for meetings with Lebanese authorities and leaders of Lebanon's Moslem communities and to Bkirke, the seat of Lebanon's Maronite Christian Patriarch northeast of the capital.
The Vatican called off a planned five-day Papal visit in May 1994 after the bombing of a Maronite church north of Beirut in which 11 Sunday worshippers were killed and 59 injured.
It has sought to play down political overtones to next weekend's visit given the opposition of many Lebanese Christians to the country's Syrian-backed government.
Cardinal Nasrallah Sfeir, the Maronite patriarch, is an outspoken critic of the government and has complained of sectarian bias by the authorities.

The Pope will meet President Elias Hrawi, a Maronite Christian, Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri, a Sunni Moslem, and Parliament Speaker Nabih Berri, a Shi'ite Moslem, at the presential palace on Saturday.
But a senior Vatican source said the weekend visit "should be seen solely as the conclusive act of the synod".
"All the rest, talk of a political visit, does not count."
The 1995 synod, closed by the Pope with an appeal for reconciliation, heard a blunt public demand from Lebanon's bishops for the withdrawal of foreign forces from the country.
Syria has an estimated 35,000 troops in Lebanon, where Israel holds a strip of territory in the south.
Vatican officials declined to say whether the Pope would explicity echo the bishops' call in a post-synodal document he will issue to mark the visit.

The document, known as an Apostolic Exhortation, will be signed by the Pope on Saturday evening at a prayer meeting with young Lebanese and published on Sunday at the end of the Pontiff's open-air mass.
The service will be held at a naval base in the war-shattered heart of the capital on the former 'Green Line' that divided Moslem West and Christian East Beirut.

The Pope's route on Saturday from the airport to Baabda will take him along the road where several foreigners were kidnapped by Shi'ite Moslem gunmen during the civil war and through areas that are strongholds of the pro-Iranian Hizbollah.

Saud Almoula, a leading Shi'ite academic, was quoted by FIDES, a Vatican news agency, as saying Moslems generally welcomed the Pope's visit as a spur to interreligious dialogue but also on national grounds.
"We Moslems are convinced that the Holy See supports Lebanon in international instances, both regarding independence (from Syrian influence) and for the cause of the south," he said.
